source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 23; printed page 1; equations (1.1)-(1.2)
source_evidence.anchor: The simplest case is the constant-coefficient scalar problem
source_evidence.observation: The scalar advection example has one spatial variable x, time t, a scalar concentration or density q(x,t), and constant fluid velocity ū. Its equation is q_t(x,t) + ū q_x(x,t) = 0.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 23; printed page 1; equation (1.3) and following paragraph
source_evidence.observation: The source asserts that q(x,t) = q̃(x − ūt) gives solutions and that the profile propagates with constant speed ū and unchanged shape.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 25; printed page 3; section 1.1; equation (1.8)
source_evidence.anchor: where f(q) is the flux function
source_evidence.observation: The conservation-law differential equation is q_t(x,t) + f(q(x,t))_x = 0.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26; printed page 4; section 1.1.1; equation (1.10)
source_evidence.anchor: for any two points x₁ and x₂
source_evidence.observation: The integral conservation equation is d/dt ∫ from x₁ to x₂ q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)). The integral represents total mass, whose change is due to flux past the endpoints.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26; printed page 4; paragraph following equation (1.10)
source_evidence.anchor: the flux function is f(q) = ūq
source_evidence.observation: For the contaminant advection example, the source identifies the linear flux f(q) = ūq and derives advection from conservation of contaminant mass.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26; printed page 4; section 1.1.2
source_evidence.anchor: provided that q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth
source_evidence.observation: Deriving the differential equation (1.8) from the integral equation (1.10) requires sufficient smoothness. Interesting solutions may instead contain discontinuities such as shock waves.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 27; printed page 5; continuation of section 1.1.2
source_evidence.anchor: does not hold in the classical sense
source_evidence.observation: At a discontinuity in q, the differential equation (1.8) does not hold classically; the source states that the more fundamental integral conservation law (1.10) continues to hold.

q(x,t) denotes scalar concentration or density in the contaminant example; q̃ specifies its spatial profile [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, discussion preceding (1.2) and following (1.3)].
The translation argument is x − ūt, with a minus sign [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, (1.3)].
f is the flux function, and for constant-velocity scalar advection f(q) = ūq [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, (1.8); raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, paragraph following (1.10)].
The spatial integral measures total conserved quantity in the interval; the right-hand side is flux at x₁ minus flux at x₂ [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, (1.10) and following explanation].

contract_plain_english: For the real, one-dimensional scalar advection equation with constant velocity ū, the source asserts that a profile q̃ generates a solution q(x,t) = q̃(x − ūt), propagating with constant speed and unchanged shape [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, (1.2)-(1.3)]. The accompanying conservation framework uses flux f(q) = ūq and balances the time change of mass in a spatial interval against flux at its first endpoint minus flux at its second [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, (1.10) and following paragraph]. Classical differential interpretation requires sufficient smoothness; at discontinuities the source retains integral conservation [raw PDF pages 26-27, printed pages 4-5, section 1.1.2]. The passage leaves the admissible class of arbitrary profiles and the precise interpretation of integral conservation for nonsmooth solutions unspecified.
